narrative:
The model predicts you have an 11% chance of failing your final year, which is low but enough for the school to require you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The prediction that you will fail is mainly driven by three key aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is that you have had no past class failures. Surprisingly, this actually pushes the model toward expecting you to fail. Among students who passed, having zero failures is the average, yet in your specific combination of circumstances the model sees this lack of past setbacks as a warning sign rather than a strength. 

The second strongest influence is your strong desire to pursue higher education. This works in your favor and pulls the prediction toward passing, which is positive since every student who passed also wanted to continue studying.

Third, your father’s secondary education level also contributes, though less strongly, and it nudges the outcome slightly toward failing. While many students who succeed have fathers with similar or lower education, the model interprets your father’s schooling, together with your other circumstances, as a mild risk.

To improve, you should focus on building consistent study habits beyond your current less-than-two-hours per week, make better use of your internet access for learning resources, and consider seeking extra academic support since you currently receive none from school or family. Taking these steps now can turn your low risk into a guaranteed success. (248 words)
